items.explanation: The burning buses and beaten riders of 1961 horrified the nation on TV — but neither Washington nor the states moved decisively to protect civil rights workers at that point.
options: A. Southerners had accepted integration orders
B. State governments enforced civil rights laws
C. Television news held a powerful grip on the public
D. Washington was committed to protecting civil rights
items.stem: The initial fate of the Freedom Riders demonstrated that

option_explanations.A: The opposite of what happened — Southerners violently resisted integration, burning the Freedom Riders' buses and beating the riders. Acceptance was nowhere in sight in 1961.
option_explanations.B: The opposite of what happened — state governments in the South protected the attackers, not the riders. Federal protection came only after the violence made national news.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The burning buses and beaten riders of 1961 horrified the nation on television — the images had a powerful grip on the public. But neither Washington nor the states moved decisively to protect civil rights workers at that point.
option_explanations.D: Washington was not yet committed to protecting civil rights workers in 1961 — the Kennedy administration intervened reluctantly and belatedly. Commitment came later, after further violence.

items.explanation: Tet was a Vietcong military disaster — but the images of fighting in Saigon and Hue proved official optimism ('victory around the corner') had been dishonest, shattering public trust.
options: A. America was near decisive victory
B. Officials had not been candid about the war
C. The Vietcong could beat Americans in battle
D. U.S.–South Vietnamese cooperation was improving

option_explanations.A: The Tet Offensive did not show America near victory — it showed the opposite. Vietcong forces struck across South Vietnam, including the U.S. embassy grounds in Saigon, demolishing claims that victory was near.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Tet was a Vietcong military disaster, but the images of fighting in Saigon and Hue proved official optimism — 'victory around the corner' — had been dishonest. The offensive shattered public trust in what officials had been saying about the war.
option_explanations.C: The Vietcong did not beat Americans in battle at Tet — they suffered devastating losses. The offensive failed militarily; its effect was psychological and political, not a battlefield triumph.
option_explanations.D: Tet did not show U.S.–South Vietnamese cooperation improving — South Vietnamese forces performed poorly and the offensive exposed the weakness of the Saigon government. Cooperation was not the story.

items.explanation: SDS peaked during the 1965–67 escalation, when the draft touched millions of students; by Cambodia (1970) and the 1972 bombing, it had splintered into factions.
options: A. The draft sent more young men to Vietnam, 1965–67
B. Southern civil rights struggles aired on TV
C. Nixon invaded Cambodia
D. Nixon's 1972 bombing peaked
items.stem: SDS membership was at its all-time high when

option_explanations.A: Correct. SDS peaked during the 1965–67 escalation, when the draft touched millions of students — membership was at its all-time high then. By the Cambodia invasion (1970) and the 1972 bombing, the organization had splintered into factions.
option_explanations.B: Southern civil rights struggles on TV mobilized many students, but they were not what drove SDS to its peak membership. The draft and the Vietnam escalation were the engines of its growth.
option_explanations.C: Nixon's invasion of Cambodia came in 1970 — after SDS had already splintered. Cambodia triggered protests, but not an SDS membership peak.
option_explanations.D: Nixon's 1972 bombing came after SDS's collapse — by then the organization had broken apart. It could not have been the moment of peak membership.

items.explanation: Northern Blacks embraced Black Power as King's integrationism seemed distant, ghettos stayed poor, and Malcolm X and Carmichael offered pride — but only a small minority actually joined the Nation of Islam.
options: A. King seemed focused on the South, not the ghetto
B. Northern ghettos remained poor and hopeless
C. Malcolm X and Carmichael evoked Black pride
D. Vast numbers joined the Nation of Islam
items.stem: Northern Blacks were drawn to 'Black Power' for all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: King really did seem focused on the South, not the Northern ghetto — a genuine reason Northern Blacks turned to Black Power. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Northern ghettos really did remain poor and hopeless — a genuine reason. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Malcolm X and Stokely Carmichael really did evoke Black pride — a genuine reason. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Correct — this is the exception. Only a small minority of Black Americans actually joined the Nation of Islam. The turn to Black Power was broad; formal membership in the Nation of Islam was not.

items.explanation: NOW, Ms. magazine, and raised consciousness of women's issues were real feminist gains — but the ERA drive died in 1982, three states short of ratification.
options: A. The founding of Ms. magazine
B. The formation of NOW
C. Ratification of the Equal Rights Amendment
D. Greater awareness of women's issues
items.stem: Feminist highlights of the era included all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: The founding of Ms. magazine (1972) really was a feminist highlight — a genuine gain. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.B: The formation of NOW (1966) really was a feminist highlight — a genuine gain. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the exception. The Equal Rights Amendment was never ratified — the drive died in 1982, three states short of the 38 needed. It was a defeat, not a highlight.
option_explanations.D: Greater awareness of women's issues really was a gain of the era — consciousness-raising was real. This is not the exception.

items.explanation: Carmichael's demand is definitional: 'whether or not black people have the right to use the words they want to use without white people giving their sanction to it' -- 'we are not going to wait for white people to sanction Black Power.' Black Power, in this speech, is the right of Black people to name their own goals, not a program of armed revolt, office-holding, or boycotts.
options: A. Black people's right to define their own goals without white approval
B. An immediate armed revolution
C. The election of Black officials exclusively
D. A nationwide economic boycott
items.stem: In the passage, Carmichael uses 'Black Power' to mean primarily
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

We are now engaged in a psychological struggle over whether Black people have the right to define themselves — to use the words they choose, to assert pride in being Black, and to demand power rather than merely beg for inclusion.
—After Stokely Carmichael, Black Power speeches, 1966–67

option_explanations.A: Correct. Carmichael's demand is definitional: whether Black people have 'the right to use the words they want to use without white people giving their sanction to it' — 'we are not going to wait for white people to sanction Black Power.' In this speech, Black Power is the right of Black people to name their own goals.
option_explanations.B: Carmichael did not call for immediate armed revolution in this speech — the demand is psychological and political (self-definition), not a call to arms.
option_explanations.C: Carmichael did not call for electing Black officials exclusively — the speech is about the right to define the struggle, not about electoral strategy.
option_explanations.D: Carmichael did not call for a nationwide economic boycott — boycotts belonged to earlier campaigns (like Montgomery). This speech is about self-definition, not boycotts.

items.explanation: The 1966 cry of 'Black Power' at the Meredith March -- and SNCC's subsequent expulsion of its white workers -- ruptured the interracial, nonviolent, integrationist coalition that King led. Carmichael was not breaking with Garvey or Washington (long dead) or with labor; he was breaking with the movement's own mainstream.
options: A. Marcus Garvey's back-to-Africa movement
B. Booker T. Washington's accommodationism
C. The organized labor movement
D. The nonviolent, integrationist civil rights mainstream
items.stem: Carmichael's 1966 call for Black Power marked a break with
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

We are now engaged in a psychological struggle over whether Black people have the right to define themselves — to use the words they choose, to assert pride in being Black, and to demand power rather than merely beg for inclusion.
—After Stokely Carmichael, Black Power speeches, 1966–67

option_explanations.A: Marcus Garvey's back-to-Africa movement was long dead by 1966 — Carmichael was not breaking with it. If anything, his Black nationalism continued Garvey's tradition.
option_explanations.B: Booker T. Washington's accommodationism was decades in the past by 1966 — Carmichael was not breaking with Washington. The break was with the movement's own living mainstream.
option_explanations.C: Carmichael was not breaking with the organized labor movement — labor was not the target of the 1966 Black Power call. The rupture was within the civil rights coalition.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The 1966 cry of 'Black Power' at the Meredith March — and SNCC's subsequent expulsion of its white workers — ruptured the interracial, nonviolent, integrationist coalition that King led. Carmichael was breaking with the movement's own mainstream.

items.explanation: Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association (1910s-20s) preached Black pride, economic self-sufficiency, and self-definition -- 'Black is beautiful' a generation early. Carmichael's insistence that Black people name their own struggle is Garvey's nationalism reborn. The NAACP's legalism, white paternalism, and Tuskegee's industrial training point the other way.
options: A. The NAACP's legal-integration strategy
B. Southern white paternalism
C. Marcus Garvey's Black nationalism
D. The Tuskegee model of industrial education
items.stem: Carmichael's emphasis on Black self-definition most directly continued the tradition of
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

We are now engaged in a psychological struggle over whether Black people have the right to define themselves — to use the words they choose, to assert pride in being Black, and to demand power rather than merely beg for inclusion.
—After Stokely Carmichael, Black Power speeches, 1966–67

option_explanations.A: The NAACP's legal-integration strategy was the opposite tradition — working through the courts for integration, not asserting separate Black self-definition. Carmichael was breaking with that approach, not continuing it.
option_explanations.B: Southern white paternalism was the enemy's tradition, not Carmichael's — whites defining what was best for Black people was exactly what he rejected.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association (1910s–20s) preached Black pride, economic self-sufficiency, and self-definition — 'Black is beautiful' a generation early. Carmichael's insistence that Black people name their own struggle is Garvey's nationalism reborn.
option_explanations.D: The Tuskegee model of industrial education was Booker T. Washington's accommodationist program — training for subservient labor, not self-definition. Carmichael's tradition is Garvey's, not Tuskegee's.
